segments.title: A routine capture with strategic consequences
segments.body: The action survives in sparse detail because it resembled a routine British success: a squadron chased down and captured five French vessels. The pursuit began on 17 June, with the firing and captures on 18 June giving the action its date. Its strategic importance lay in the shrinking French naval presence after the Battle of the Nile. Nelson was absent, leaving the capable Lord Keith to direct the fleet and detach the pursuing squadron. British accounts reduce the ending to the French ships striking, while some French accounts present the surrender more heroically. Faced with ships of the line and a decisive battery mismatch, rapid surrender was an understandable choice. Repeated losses of this kind reduced the forces available for French policy in the Mediterranean.

evidence.note: The introduction contrasts the action's sparse record and limited fighting with its effect on French Mediterranean policy.

segments.summary: The capture of five French vessels on 18 June 1799 weakened an already depleted naval presence in the Mediterranean after the Battle of the Nile.

segments.title: The Second Coalition and cumulative naval losses
segments.body: The War of the Second Coalition found France successful on land and increasingly constrained at sea. Britain, Austria, Russia, the Ottoman Empire, Portugal, Naples, and several German monarchies opposed France, while Spain fought alongside the French and Prussia stayed outside this coalition. Earlier defeats and blockade had already eroded French training and experience before Trafalgar. Losses among lieutenants, midshipmen, petty officers, and pursers damaged navigation, seamanship, administration, and fleet logistics. Pursers were especially important to outfitting ships and getting a fleet to sea. Revolutionary political removals compounded the loss of skilled personnel in battle. Slower preparation then made blockade easier, while tighter blockade denied replacement crews the sea time needed to become effective sailors.

evidence.note: The transcript connects the Second Coalition, the Nile, blockade, and personnel attrition to French institutional decline before Trafalgar.

segments.summary: Repeated defeats, blockade, and personnel losses steadily stripped the French Navy of the experience needed to challenge Britain at sea.

segments.title: How early naval losses compound across wars
segments.body: A naval loss keeps shaping operations long after the immediate action. The loss of HMS Courageous and HMS Glorious continued to constrain British naval operations during the Second World War. Pearl Harbor adds another example, pairing damage to the battle fleet with limitations on tanker deployments. Perrée's later defeat can be read in the same way, as a loss of crews, logistical capacity, and future operational choices.

evidence.note: The transcript uses Courageous, Glorious, and Pearl Harbor to explain the cumulative operational effects of naval losses.

segments.summary: Courageous, Glorious, and Pearl Harbor provide cross-era examples of how an early loss narrows a navy's options long after the immediate action.

segments.title: Napoleon's expedition after the Battle of the Nile
segments.body: The campaign began with the seizure of Malta and a successful passage to Egypt, combining amphibious manoeuvre with judgment and luck. Malta was a prestigious gain, but French control of the island proved vulnerable without command of the surrounding sea. After the Battle of the Nile, Nelson released French sailors rather than undertake the burden of feeding them as prisoners. Napoleon therefore had sailors without their battle fleet, many lacking the equipment and infantry training needed for land warfare. He employed some in small craft on the Nile and used the remaining frigates to assist the army. Their naval 18-pounders were substantial siege weapons by army standards, although an 18-pounder was an ordinary main gun for a frigate.

evidence.note: The expedition takes Malta and reaches Egypt, followed by the release and employment of French sailors after the Nile and the army use of frigate 18-pounders.

segments.summary: The French expedition reached Egypt through bold amphibious maneuver, but the Nile left Napoleon with stranded sailors and only a few frigates for support.

segments.title: Perrée's squadron stripped for siege support
segments.body: Rear Admiral Jean-Baptiste Perrée's three frigates and two brigs carried cargo between the Nile and Jaffa and supplied guns for the Siege of Acre. Junon landed four 18-pounders, while the squadron surrendered so much ammunition to the army that only about fifteen rounds remained per gun. Continued fire support would deplete that allowance further. Tying cruising ships to predictable army-support routes made them easier for British forces to find, without giving them enough firepower to withstand interception. When Sidney Smith appeared with two ships of the line and a frigate, Perrée could neither defeat him nor safely remain on station. His orders allowed a return to Europe only if unavoidable, but depleted food, water, and ammunition persuaded him and his officers that they had to leave. They chose Toulon as their destination, with a planned stop at Lampedusa to replenish water.

evidence.note: Perrée supports Jaffa and Acre with guns and ammunition, leaving fifteen rounds per gun, then decides with his officers to return to Toulon via Lampedusa under pressure from Smith.
The comparison with Markham notes that further fire support would consume the already reduced ammunition allowance.

segments.summary: Five French frigates and brigs supported the army until landed guns, scarce ammunition, and depleted supplies made continued operations untenable.

segments.title: Perrée and the French Navy's experience gap
segments.body: Perrée went to sea at twelve under his father in the merchant service and earned a merchant captain's commission in 1785. He joined the navy in 1793, and his early record included an inconclusive action against Horatio Nelson and subsequent commerce raiding. He reached captain in September 1794 and rear admiral by 1799. His ability and long experience at sea made him valuable, but his senior naval rank rested on only a few years of naval service. That rapid promotion reflected shortages caused by revolutionary upheaval, wartime losses, and earlier royal policy. The expulsion of Huguenot and Protestant officers had already cost France experienced personnel, many of whom carried their skills into British service.

evidence.note: The transcript traces Perrée's merchant background, wartime promotion, and what it reveals about French officer shortages.

segments.summary: Perrée was an able and experienced merchant sailor, but his rapid rise to rear admiral exposed the revolutionary navy's shortage of trained naval officers.

segments.title: Keith, Markham, and Royal Navy continuity
segments.body: Lord Keith brought experience spanning the Seven Years' War, the American Revolutionary War, and the wars with France. His biography also distinguishes the viscountcy that ended at his death from the British and Irish baronies inherited by his eldest daughter Margaret, which ended at hers. John Markham, like Perrée, was born in 1761, but had served in the Royal Navy since 1775, when he was fourteen. He spent those years learning to navigate and fight naval ships, while most of Perrée's earlier experience came from merchant service. Markham later became an admiral, MP for Portsmouth, and First Naval Lord under St Vincent. Their careers show the difference between general seagoing experience and sustained preparation for naval command. A hypothetical comparison suggests that Markham might have found a way around orders to leave only fifteen rounds per gun aboard a squadron still expected to provide fire support. That imagined response contrasts with Perrée's literal obedience; it is not an incident attributed to Markham's actual service.

evidence.note: The lecture profiles Keith and Markham and contrasts Markham's continuous naval formation with Perrée's merchant background.

segments.summary: Lord Keith and John Markham had spent decades in naval service, giving the British squadron an experience base that Perrée's rapidly promoted French command could not match.

segments.title: Junon from French frigate to British veteran
segments.body: Junon was a Minerve-class frigate of roughly 700 tons, armed in French service with twenty-eight 18-pounders and twelve 8-pounders. At least four of the 18-pounders had been landed to assist the army before the action. Ordered in 1781, she was laid down and launched in 1782 but did not commission until 1786, an interval associated here with French preparation delays. Captured after thirteen years of French service, she became HMS Princess Charlotte and was renamed Andromache in 1812. The Royal Navy retained her until she was broken up in 1828, giving her twenty-nine years under British ownership and employing her extensively. Lord Keith used the ship again in 1812. A description attributed to him praises her as a fusion of British and French construction, but that attribution comes from a source explicitly treated as too unreliable for unqualified academic use.

evidence.note: Junon is identified as a Minerve-class frigate with reduced armament, followed through British renamings and service to 1828, and discussed with a caveat about the praise attributed to Keith.

segments.summary: The Minerve-class Junon entered the action short of guns, then enjoyed a much longer career under British names after capture.

segments.title: Centaur and Courageuse reveal the firepower mismatch
segments.body: HMS Centaur was a 74-gun third rate carrying twenty-eight 32-pounders, thirty 24-pounders, and sixteen 9-pounders. Her career also included the Diamond Rock operation off Martinique. British support to an army could include landed guns and their ammunition, while retaining the ammunition for the guns left aboard. Perrée's ships had instead lost weapons and much of the ammunition needed by their remaining batteries. Courageuse was a Concorde-class frigate with twenty-six 12-pounders and six 6-pounders, leaving her badly outmatched by Centaur's heavier guns. The modern Hermione reconstruction, built at Rochefort from 1997 and launched in 2012, follows the same class's lines and provides a visual reference for this type of French frigate. The comparison explains why a frigate could not exchange fire with a ship of the line on equal terms.

evidence.note: The transcript compares Centaur's heavy battery and ammunition policy with the Concorde-class frigate's lighter guns.

segments.summary: Comparing a British 74-gun ship with a French 12-pounder frigate makes clear why the French squadron could not fight on equal terms.

segments.title: Bellona, Captain, and the 74-gun standard
segments.body: Thomas Slade's Bellona design became a model for the Royal Navy's 74-gun third rates and several closely related classes. Bellona carried twenty-eight 32-pounders on the lower deck and twenty-eight 18-pounders on the upper deck, with fourteen 9-pounders on the quarterdeck and four on the forecastle. A French frigate might match the weight of Bellona's 18-pounder shot, but still had to face the much heavier lower battery. HMS Captain carried the same combination and numbers of long guns. Captain had already been associated with Nelson's boarding of larger ships before serving in this pursuit. Sir Richard Strachan is suggested as Captain's commander for the action, with explicit uncertainty about the command chronology. Whatever that attribution, the British squadron had several ships whose batteries individually overwhelmed the lighter French vessels.

evidence.note: Bellona is presented as a model 74 with twenty-eight 32-pounders, twenty-eight 18-pounders, and sixteen 9-pounders.
Captain has the same battery, a connection to Nelson boarding first rates, and an explicitly uncertain attribution of command to Sir Richard Strachan.

segments.summary: Bellona and Captain brought the standard 74-gun combination of 32-pounder and 18-pounder batteries against French frigates and brigs.

segments.title: Alceste's changing owners and light battery
segments.body: Alceste passed from France to the Kingdom of Sardinia and back to France before her British capture. She was ordered, laid down, and launched in 1780, then commissioned in 1781. Her listed battery comprised twenty-six 12-pounder long guns and six 6-pounders. That light armament left her unable to match Bellona, the 74-gun ship identified as her opponent in the coming action.

evidence.note: Alceste changes national service, is built in 1780 and commissioned in 1781, carries twenty-six 12-pounders and six 6-pounders, and is matched against Bellona.

segments.summary: Alceste passed between French and Sardinian service before facing Bellona with a battery centred on 12-pounders.

segments.title: Salamine, the Spanish brig renamed for Salamis
segments.body: Salamine began in Spanish service as Infante and was captured by the French in December 1793. She received the name Salamine in May 1798, commemorating the Battle of Salamis. Her armament is described as eighteen 6-pounders. That battery explains the brig's difficulty when a full-sized British frigate became her pursuer: the equal number of vessels on each side concealed very unequal fighting power.

evidence.note: Salamine is identified as the former Spanish Infante, captured in December 1793, renamed in May 1798 after Salamis, and armed with eighteen 6-pounders.
The comparison contrasts three French frigates with British third rates and the two small brigs with full-sized British frigates.

segments.summary: Captured from Spain as Infante, Salamine carried eighteen 6-pounders and faced a British frigate with a much heavier battery.

segments.title: Emerald's battery and long cruising career
segments.body: HMS Emerald was an Amazon-class sailing frigate ordered and laid down in 1794, launched and commissioned in 1795, and retained until she was broken up in January 1836. Her gun deck carried twenty-six 18-pounder long guns. The quarterdeck added eight 9-pounders and six 32-pounder carronades, with two more of each type on the forecastle. Her career included the action of 26 April 1797, the bombardment of Cadiz, the attack on Santa Cruz, and duty off Alexandria. After the June 1799 captures, she also took part in the action of 7 April 1800, the capture of Suriname, and operations in home waters and at the Basque Roads. That range of service illustrates the repeated demands placed on a cruising frigate and the heavy armament brought against the French brigs.

evidence.note: Emerald's construction and disposal dates, Amazon class, long-gun and carronade battery, and varied operational career are described.

segments.summary: Emerald combined 18-pounder long guns and 32-pounder carronades with a career spanning Mediterranean, Atlantic, and home-water operations.

segments.title: Alerte's repeated capture and uncertain armament
segments.body: Alerte had already been captured by the British in 1793, when she carried ten 4-pounder guns. The British subsequently burned her, and the French salvaged and rebuilt the brig for further service. Her battery at the 1799 capture is uncertain: fourteen 6-pounders is the working estimate, with a possibility that some 4-pounder armament remained. This distinction matters when comparing her with the pursuing British ships, since even the heavier proposed battery was very light. The 1799 action was another capture in a career that had already involved loss, salvage, and reconstruction.

evidence.note: Alerte's uncertain 1799 armament is compared with her ten 4-pounders at the earlier capture, followed by British burning and French salvage and rebuilding.

segments.summary: The French salvaged and rebuilt Alerte after an earlier British capture and burning, only to lose the brig again in 1799.

segments.title: Santa Teresa and the informal economy of blockade
segments.body: HMS Santa Teresa had been captured from Spain in February 1799, although the ship's surviving description and illustrations proved difficult to trace. John Markham's earlier account of blockade duty under St Vincent supplies a more detailed example of British dealings with Spain. Spanish intermediaries arranged for officers' linen to be washed in the town they were blockading. Officers also received fresh beef, mutton, fowl, eggs, and vegetables from Portugal and Tangier through these contacts. Formal hostility therefore coexisted with local exchange that helped sustain the blockading fleet.

evidence.note: The transcript notes Santa Teresa's obscurity and quotes Markham on provisions and laundry obtained while blockading Spain.

segments.summary: Santa Teresa's capture in February 1799 and Markham's account of Spanish supply contacts show different ways Britain benefited from its opponent's resources.

segments.title: The official dispatch reduces the action to a chase
segments.body: The London Gazette prints St Vincent's covering letter from Port Mahon, dated 22 June 1799, forwarding reports written by Keith and Markham on 19 June. Keith praises Markham, whose ship was furthest advanced, while Markham describes a general chase to the northeast and the capture of three frigates. Bellona and Santa Teresa were nearest when the first two struck, so he signalled them to take possession while he pursued the third. Emerald took Salamine and Captain took Alerte. The accompanying list records the French squadron's reported guns and crews, and the letter describes it as thirty-three days out from Jaffa, bound for Toulon. The report says little about fighting beyond the ships striking, leaving the timing and conduct of the action to be reconstructed from other accounts.

evidence.note: The transcript reads the Keith and Markham correspondence and the accompanying French force list.

segments.summary: Keith and Markham's dispatches record the capture in terse sequence and list the French squadron's reported guns and crews.

segments.title: The twenty-eight-hour chase toward Toulon
segments.body: The French were roughly sixty miles from Toulon when Lord Keith's fleet, described as about thirty ships, found them. The estimate of less than a day's sailing to safety assumes better progress than they could necessarily make in the prevailing wind. Keith lacked enough admirals for every detachment and used the senior captain Markham in a commodore's role. Markham pursued with three ships of the line and two frigates, a force that matched the French squadron in hull numbers while greatly exceeding its firepower. A weak southwesterly wind stretched the chase through the night and into a second evening, for about twenty-eight hours. Both forces had to extract what speed they could before the British were close enough to use their guns.

evidence.note: The transcript estimates the distance from Toulon, identifies the detached British force, and describes the weak wind and 28-hour pursuit.

segments.summary: Only about sixty miles from Toulon, Perrée's dispersed squadron endured a twenty-eight-hour chase in weak wind before the British ships closed.

segments.title: Five surrenders in four and a half hours
segments.body: Around 7 p.m., Bellona closed to about a quarter mile from Junon and opened fire, prompting Junon and Alceste to strike almost immediately. Perrée had tried to escape and waited for British fire before surrendering; the interpretation is that this satisfied naval honour before the court-martial he expected after capture. The French squadron had become widely separated, with Courageuse about a mile farther on and the brigs roughly four to seven miles ahead of Junon. Centaur continued after Courageuse, which tried to fight until Bellona joined and made the mismatch two 74s against one frigate. Emerald caught Salamine, while Captain crowded on sail to overtake Alerte, completing the captures around 11:30 p.m. The four-and-a-half-hour action consisted chiefly of successive pursuits and surrenders, following the much longer chase.

evidence.note: Bellona closes at about 7 p.m., Junon and Alceste strike after British fire, the dispersed remaining vessels are pursued separately, and Alerte surrenders around 11:30 p.m.

segments.summary: Junon and Alceste struck first, Courageuse yielded to two 74s, and the British frigate and ship of the line overhauled the fleeing brigs.

segments.title: Why contemporary gun and crew counts disagree
segments.body: The London Gazette's force list gives Junon forty guns and 500 men, while Lloyd's List gives forty-four guns and 560 men. Alceste appears with thirty-six guns in both lists, but with 300 men in the Gazette and 460 in Lloyd's. Lloyd's also reports Courageuse with forty-four guns and 500 men, well above the thirty-two-gun battery described earlier. The Gazette lists Salamine with eighteen guns and Alerte with fourteen, whereas Lloyd's gives each sixteen. These are competing contemporary reports, so their figures cannot all be treated as precise statements of strength at capture. The disagreement warrants caution about individual totals without obscuring the much larger mismatch between frigates, brigs, and ships of the line.

evidence.note: The Gazette force list gives the French ships' reported guns and crews.
Lloyd's List gives different gun and crew totals, and the two contemporary reports are explicitly compared.
Courageuse's class battery is described as twenty-six 12-pounders and six 6-pounders.

segments.summary: Lloyd's List and the London Gazette give different strengths for the same captured ships, limiting how precisely the forces can be reconstructed.

segments.title: Why five cruising ships mattered
segments.body: Richard Harding's force figures divide the fleets into line-of-battle ships and smaller cruising warships. Treating third rates and larger ships as 'battleships' and fourth rates and smaller vessels as 'cruisers' is a rough interpretation for strategic comparison, with an explicitly uncertain cutoff. French and allied cruising strength peaked at roughly 144 vessels in 1796, fell to about 90 by 1800, and reached 71 by 1805. Britain maintained roughly 158 to 160 cruising ships from 1796 to 1805. By 1805 Britain also had about 136 commissioned third rates and larger ships, against 96 for France and its allies. Losing five cruising vessels together removed trained crews and scarce ships needed for scouting, escort, and communications from a navy already short of them.

evidence.note: Harding's figures support a rough division between line-of-battle and cruising ships, followed by the 1796 and 1800 totals and the effect of losing five vessels and crews.
The comparison supplies the 1805 totals of 160 British and 71 French and allied cruising ships, and 136 versus 96 third rates and larger ships.
Frigates provide information, presence, fleet communication, and escort for supply ships.

segments.summary: France and its allies lost five scarce cruising ships and their crews while Britain's strength in smaller warships remained comparatively steady.

segments.title: Prisoner exchanges and the war for naval experience
segments.body: Perrée's senior rank made him comparatively easy to exchange because France lacked ships for him to command. British authorities placed more value on retaining navigators, junior officers, petty officers, and trained sailors. Those ranks carried the practical knowledge needed to prepare, navigate, and fight a fleet. In this reading, French political leaders undervalued those skills, allowing captivity to compound the navy's existing loss of institutional memory.

evidence.note: The transcript explains why Britain exchanged Perrée quickly but preferred to retain French navigators, junior officers, petty officers, and sailors.

segments.summary: British prisoner policy targeted the navigators and junior officers France needed to rebuild an effective seagoing institution.

segments.title: Perrée's acquittal and the captured ships' careers
segments.body: Perrée underwent a court-martial from 6 October to 25 November 1799. The court accepted superior Ottoman-British forces in Syria, partial disarmament, and low food and water supplies as legitimate reasons to return to Toulon, and honourably acquitted him. Junon entered British service as Princess Charlotte, Courageuse became a prison hulk at Minorca or, more likely, Malta, and Alceste became a floating battery. The two brigs also entered British service, with Salamine capturing privateers in the Mediterranean. After the Treaty of Amiens in 1802, Britain disposed of Alceste, Alerte, and Salamine. Those disposals did not prevent British cruising strength from growing toward 1805.

evidence.note: The lecture describes Perrée's acquittal and summarizes the captured ships' Royal Navy uses and disposal.

segments.summary: A French court accepted Perrée's reasons for retreat and surrender, while Britain retained, repurposed, or later disposed of the captured vessels.

segments.title: Why a distant interception protected Britain's blockade
segments.body: Even a French-Spanish victory at Trafalgar would probably have left a damaged fleet facing further British squadrons farther north. Its survival in those later encounters is posed as an open question. Intercepting the enemy far from Britain reduced the need to divert close-blockading forces to meet a threat nearer home. Maintaining those blockades sustained economic pressure on France; relaxing them would have prolonged the war in this interpretation. The French shortage of frigates made that wider contest harder, despite their limited ability to fight ships of the line directly.

evidence.note: The counterfactual of a French-Spanish Trafalgar victory leads to the argument for distant interception, uninterrupted blockade, economic pressure, and the consequences of French frigate shortages.

segments.summary: The Trafalgar counterfactual asks whether a damaged victorious fleet could survive further British interception, then explains why Britain wanted to fight far from its blockade stations.

segments.title: Frigates sustain blockade, supply, and information
segments.body: Frigates supplied information, presence, and communications, and escorted the provision convoys that kept blockading squadrons at sea. Ships in the Channel Squadron commonly remained out for twenty weeks, with some reaching twenty-three weeks. They could not do this without receiving supplies, even though ships also returned to places such as Torbay for repair, refit, and replenishment. Frigates escorted the supply ships in convoys moving between the fleet and its bases. Ships of the line travelling back to the fleet could accompany these convoys while retaining independent orders. That distinction allowed them to leave the convoy and rejoin the fleet quickly when the situation required it. A frigate shortage therefore affected the supply and coordination of the whole fleet.

evidence.note: Frigates provide information and communications and escort supply convoys for ships spending twenty to twenty-three weeks at sea, while accompanying ships of the line retain independent orders.

segments.summary: Frigates mattered as fleet scouts, messengers, presence ships, and escorts for the supply convoys that kept blockading squadrons at sea.

segments.title: Egypt versus Gibraltar as Napoleon's strategic choice
segments.body: Napoleon's army and fleet invite a counterfactual question: would reinforcing Spain and attacking Gibraltar have achieved more than the expedition to Egypt? His artillery background gives some grounds for imagining a successful attack, without making the outcome certain. Losing Gibraltar could have complicated British access to the Mediterranean during the remaining Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars. The proposed onward campaign toward India raises a separate difficulty: where would the ships come from to carry it there? Egypt's prestige is another possible explanation for the choice, left unresolved. The closing discussion prompt also offers Sicily and Naples as alternative Mediterranean targets for comparison.

evidence.note: The conclusion questions Egypt's strategic purpose, considers reinforcing Spain to attack Gibraltar, and asks how a campaign toward India would obtain naval transport.
The closing question invites comparison of Egyptian, Sicilian, and Neapolitan targets without a recorded audience response.

segments.summary: Attacking Gibraltar with Spanish support is considered as an alternative to Napoleon's Egyptian expedition and its uncertain onward route to India.

segments.title: Why Perrée's crews could not make the escape work
segments.body: Perrée and Markham both tried to get the most from their ships, but the French squadron began the chase in worse material condition. Its ships were inadequately cleaned, maintained, and equipped, and their frigate batteries were outgunned by three British third rates. Perrée tried the sailing expedients available to him during the twenty-eight-hour chase. His crews lacked the practice needed to execute them as effectively as British crews, who could crowd on sail and maintain pursuit. The outcome depended on ship condition and practised collective seamanship as well as each commander's judgement.

evidence.note: The closing assessment credits both commanders' efforts while contrasting French material condition and crew experience with British ability to execute sailing manoeuvres throughout the chase.

segments.summary: Poor material condition and limited crew experience prevented Perrée's sailing manoeuvres from defeating a prolonged British pursuit.
